result.summary: The Spartans, encouraged by good sacrifices, march on Ithome while the Messenians' allies lag behind. In a drawn battle King Euphaes is mortally wounded, and after his death Aristodemus is elected king despite the seers' objection. The war continues with raids on both sides.

scenes.title: Sparta marches on Ithome
scenes.summary: The Spartans, once discouraged by the oracle, attack Ithome in the sixth year after Lyciscus fled. Cretan, Argive and Arcadian allies are late, but the Messenians trust the oracle and fight anyway.
scenes.stakes: The Messenians risk defeat without their allies; the Spartans risk another failed campaign.

scenes.title: Battle and death of Euphaes
scenes.summary: The battle ends at nightfall with the best men fighting in the centre. Euphaes is gravely wounded, saved by his men, and dies after thirteen years as king; Antander is killed.
scenes.stakes: Euphaes risks his life, and the Messenians risk disgrace if they abandon their king.

scenes.title: Aristodemus elected king
scenes.summary: The people choose Aristodemus over Cleonnis and Damis, although the seers call him polluted by his daughter's murder. He rewards the people and cultivates allies.
scenes.stakes: The kingdom may be tainted by Aristodemus's pollution, as the seers warn.

scenes.title: Raids and Argive caution
scenes.summary: Both sides pillage in summer, with Arcadians and Messenians raiding Laconia. The Argives prepare quietly without declaring hostility.
scenes.stakes: Laconia faces raids; the Argives risk open conflict with Sparta.

analysis.text: Piety and pollution matter in politics: the seers object to Aristodemus on religious grounds, yet the people elect him.
The passage reflects the shifting alliances of Peloponnesian states against Spartan power in the First Messenian War.

language_notes.text: "Auspicious" sacrifices means the omens from the offerings were favourable, giving the Spartans religious permission to march.
"Behindhand" means late or behind schedule; the allied contingents had not yet arrived.
"Rival competitors with Aristodemus" means they stood against him for the kingship, though judged his betters in war and otherwise.
Aristodemus had earlier sacrificed his daughter in obedience to an oracle, which the seers regard as blood-pollution; Æpytus was an ancient Messenian royal ancestor.
"Strike in when the fray begun" means join the fighting once it was well under way, without committing early.

context_notes.text: The oracle, given to the Messenians, had apparently promised them success, which discouraged Sparta's kings and people.
Theopompus was a Spartan king, so Euphaes, the Messenian king, charges directly at the enemy's commander.
Arcadians were neighbours of Sparta and sometimes hostile to it, so Aristodemus courts their leaders as allies.

literary_notes.text: The bravest men crowding into the centre gives a vivid picture of battle, with the "strain of battle" concentrated at one point.
The Messenians' loyalty shows their devotion to Euphaes, and the narrator frames their honour as stronger than self-preservation.
Aristodemus is chosen despite the seers' warning and despite being thought inferior, an uneasy beginning that foreshadows his troubled reign.
